title: In Defence of Fan Fiction
paragraphs: When I tell people that I write fan fiction, I usually notice a polite pause, as if I had confessed to a minor crime. I am nineteen, I study engineering in Monterrey, and for six years I have been writing long stories about characters invented by other people. I have never earned a single peso from it, and I have no intention of changing that.

Critics say it is lazy: if you can't invent your own characters, they argue, you are not a real writer. But this misunderstands how writing is learned. Musicians begin by playing other people's songs, a painter copies a masterpiece in a museum, and nobody calls them thieves. Borrowing a world is a way of studying how it was built.

Fan fiction taught me more than any class. To write a scene in the style of a novelist I admire, I had to understand why her sentences were short when the characters were frightened, and long when they were calm. I learned to build tension, to end a chapter at the right moment, and to accept criticism from readers who did not hesitate to tell me where my plot made no sense.

There is also the community. Most of my readers are strangers who live in other countries; one of them, a retired nurse in Chile, has commented on nearly every chapter for three years. We have never met, yet she is among the people who know my writing best. That kind of attention is rare for beginners, and it is a powerful motivator.

Of course, there are problems. Some stories are badly written, and some are inappropriate for younger readers, which is why good archives add a clear warning. There are also legitimate questions about the rights of the original authors. Many authors accept fan works as long as nobody sells them, but a few object, and their wishes must be respected.

Still, I would argue that the benefits outweigh the risks. If a teacher discovered that a student had written two hundred thousand words in his free time, she would call him dedicated. The fact that the words happen to involve a wizard school or a space crew should not change that judgement.

title: The Café Where Nothing Is Thrown Away
paragraphs: On the first Saturday of every month, the community centre of a Rotterdam neighbourhood fills with the sound of screwdrivers. Tables are covered with broken toasters, torn jackets, wobbly chairs and one very old radio. Nothing here is thrown away. Instead, volunteers examine each object and, if possible, fix it for free.

The Repair Café, as it is called, was started by a group of residents who were tired of seeing perfectly good things end up in the bin. 'A lamp stops working, and people just buy a new one,' says Henk de Vries, a retired electrician who has volunteered since the beginning. 'But most of the time the problem is a small wire. Five minutes, and it's finished.'

Visitors are not expected to watch passively. They sit beside the repairer, hold the tools and learn as the work proceeds. Amina El Idrissi, nineteen, brought a broken hairdryer last spring and has been returning ever since, this time as a volunteer. 'I came for the hairdryer,' she laughs, 'and I stayed because I realised that I enjoyed understanding how things work.'

The financial benefit is real, although modest. A new vacuum cleaner can cost over a hundred euros, while a repair here costs only the price of the replacement part, usually a couple of euros. The environmental benefit is harder to measure, yet the organisers calculate that the café has kept about one tonne of electrical waste out of the rubbish dump in the last year.

Not every object can be saved. Phones, in particular, are often sealed with glue so that repairers cannot open them without breaking them. Henk finds this frustrating. 'Some products seem designed to fail,' he says. 'We do what we can, but we're fighting against the manufacturers.' He believes that laws should oblige companies to make their products repairable.

At four o'clock, the volunteers are tired, and most tables are empty. A man leaves with a working radio and a wide smile; a girl goes away carrying a repaired jacket, with a bright yellow patch on one elbow. 'It looks better than before,' she announces. Henk, packing his tools, agrees. 'That's the secret,' he says. 'Sometimes a repair makes a thing more yours than a new one ever could.'

title: Review: Pueblo Hondo, Mendoza
paragraphs: Reaching Pueblo Hondo, a restaurant forty minutes from the centre of Mendoza, requires a rented car, a good map and a certain faith in your driver. It is worth the effort. Set among vines, with the Andes behind it like a painted backdrop, it is the kind of place where you forget to check your phone. The restaurant has only twelve tables, and the kitchen is open so that diners can see the cooks at work.

The menu is short: five starters, six mains and three desserts, all prepared with ingredients grown within a few kilometres. We began with grilled cheese made from goat's milk, served with a sweet tomato jam, which was a perfect balance of salty and sweet. My friend Julián, who normally ignores vegetables, finished the roasted carrots and asked for more bread to clean the plate.

The main courses were less consistent. My slow-cooked lamb, falling off the bone and served with a smoky potato purée, was easily the best dish of the evening. By contrast, Julián's trout was slightly overcooked, and the sauce, though attractive, was a little too sharp. Our waitress, Lorena, noticed his hesitation and offered to bring something else. That small gesture said a lot about the restaurant's attitude.

Wine, naturally, is the main attraction. The list features local producers, and the staff don't simply recommend the most expensive bottle. Lorena suggested a modest Malbec from a family vineyard, and it matched the lamb beautifully. Visitors who don't drink alcohol can enjoy an excellent grape juice, pressed on the premises.

A word of warning: the restaurant is popular, and the service, while friendly, can be slow when every table is full. We waited almost forty minutes between the starters and the mains. Booking is essential, and I would advise arriving hungry and without any plans for the rest of the afternoon.

Prices are fair for the quality, with main dishes at around fifteen thousand pesos, and the dessert, a warm quince tart with ice cream, deserved more than the single spoon we shared. Despite the slow pace and the uneven fish, I left happy and already planning my return. Four stars out of five.

title: A Robot Built from a Broken Fan
paragraphs: Rodrigo Mamani is seventeen and captain of his school's robotics team in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. Last month, the team built a robot that collects plastic bottles from the school playground. We asked him how a group of teenagers with a small budget achieved it.
Q: Where did the idea come from?

A: From a very ordinary problem. After break every day, the playground was covered with bottles, and the cleaner needed an hour to pick them up. One of our team, Daniela, said as a joke that a robot could do it. Nobody laughed. We looked at each other and thought: why not?
Q: What was the biggest obstacle?

A: Money. Our budget was about eight hundred bolivianos, which is almost nothing for electronics. We used old motors from a broken fan and wheels from a toy truck, and a parent who works at a repair shop gave us a battery. Without those donations, we would have given up in the first month.
Q: Did it work immediately?

A: Not at all. The first version drove in circles for two weeks. Eventually we found that one wheel was turning faster than the other, and that was because I had connected two cables the wrong way. It was embarrassing, but also hilarious, and the team never let me forget it.
Q: What have you learned about teamwork?

A: That arguing is normal. We had huge arguments about the design. In the end, we agreed to test every idea, instead of voting, and let the results decide. If I had insisted on my own design, the robot would have been slower, and I would never have known. I used to think leaders always had the best ideas; now I think a leader's job is to listen.
Q: What is next?

A: We are working on a version with a camera, so that it can recognise bottles and ignore other objects. We also want to teach younger students, because our team has only eight members, and half of us will leave school next year. Somebody has to keep the project alive. We also want to give the robot a name that is not 'Robot Number One'. Suggestions are welcome.

title: The Myth of Talent
paragraphs: 'You're so talented!' It is one of the most flattering sentences in the language, and one of the most dangerous. When we say it, we mean to give a compliment. What we often communicate, however, is that the skill is a gift that some people have and others don't, like green eyes.

The belief that talent is fixed is widespread, and it affects the way we learn. A student who thinks that mathematics is 'not for him' will give up after the first difficult page, convinced that effort is useless. By contrast, a student who sees ability as something that grows with practice is more likely to treat a mistake as information, not as a verdict. Research on motivation, though still developing, points in the same direction.

This does not mean that all people start from the same point. Differences in height, memory and even temperament are real, and they sometimes give a person an early advantage. But an early advantage is not the same as long-term success. Many children who are praised as prodigies lose interest as soon as the work becomes demanding, while others, who seemed ordinary at ten, become excellent at twenty because they never stopped.

Take the example of a girl I know who learned to play the violin. At the beginning, her teacher thought she had little rhythm, and she herself was ready to quit. Her uncle, a plumber, offered a different view: 'Nobody is born with a violin in their hands.' She practised for twenty minutes a day, every day, for four years. Today she plays in a youth orchestra, and she is frequently complimented on her 'natural' ear.

That final word is what bothers me. 'Natural' hides the four years. It tells the listener that the music appeared from nowhere, and it makes the next beginner feel worse about her own awkward first attempts. If we chose to praise the process instead, by saying, 'You've clearly worked hard on that passage,' we would send a more useful message.

Perhaps we should retire the word 'talent', or at least use it more carefully. It describes a beginning, not a destination. What happens between the two depends on time, patience and the courage to sound bad for a while.

title: The Night Shift
focus: Past continuous, past perfect and reported speech
paragraphs: Facundo had been working the night shift at his uncle's pharmacy in Buenos Aires for exactly three weeks when the strange customer arrived. It was a quarter to three in the morning, and the street outside was empty except for a taxi that was waiting with its engine running. Facundo, who was supposed to be studying for his university entrance exam, was instead drawing a cartoon on the back of a receipt.

The man who came in was old, tall and thin, wearing a coat that was far too heavy for the weather. He did not ask for medicine. 'I need to know,' he said slowly, 'whether this pharmacy sells the small blue cough syrup. The one with the picture of a lion.' Facundo checked the shelves. They had never stocked it. 'It was discontinued years ago,' he explained.

The man's face fell. 'My wife used to give it to our son every winter,' he said. 'She died in July, and I wanted to taste it again, just once.' He laughed at himself, a little embarrassed. 'It's a silly thing to want at three in the morning.' Facundo, who had been about to suggest that he come back in the morning, felt the words disappear.

'It's not silly,' Facundo said. He remembered the lion on the bottle, because his own grandmother had bought the same syrup, and he told the man so. They spent the next twenty minutes talking about winters in their childhoods, about wooden floors and noisy radiators and the taste of cherry flavouring. Facundo gave him a different syrup, a plain one, and said that it was not the same, but that it was made for the same reason: to make someone feel better.

The man insisted on paying. When he left, Facundo discovered that he had put a few notes under the receipt on the counter, far more than the syrup cost. He ran to the door, but the taxi was already turning the corner.

For days afterwards, Facundo kept the money in an envelope, unsure what to do. In the end, he spent it on a notebook, a proper one, and he stopped drawing on receipts. On the first page, he wrote the first lines of a story about a pharmacist who sells memories. He passed his exam in December, though not with a high mark. The notebook, however, he kept on the counter, beside a postcard that had arrived in January from a seaside town, with a small lion drawn in the corner and a single word: 'Gracias'.

title: Noise in the School Library: Findings
paragraphs: ## Purpose

This report examines the level of noise in the library of Colegio San Rafael in Asunción, Paraguay, after students made a formal complaint about it. Many of them use the library for homework and exam revision.
## Method

Noise was measured with a free smartphone application over five school days. Readings were taken at three times (before school, during the lunch break and after classes) in two areas: the reading room and the computer corner. We are aware that a phone microphone is less precise than professional equipment, so the figures are best seen as a comparison between times and places, not as exact values. Student behaviour was also observed by two volunteers sitting at the back of the room.
## Findings

The reading room was generally quiet before school and after classes, with an average level similar to a quiet office. During the lunch break, however, the level was noticeably higher, comparable to a busy restaurant. The computer corner was the noisiest area at every time of day. The volunteers noted that most of the noise came from group conversations, not from individual students, and that the librarian asked for silence about four times during the lunch break, usually with little effect.

A short questionnaire answered by 45 students showed that 31 of them (69 per cent) considered the library 'too noisy' at lunch time, and 38 (84 per cent) said they would use it more often if there were a silent zone.
## Recommendations

We recommend dividing the library into two zones: a silent zone for individual study, and a discussion zone for group work. A simple sign and a low bookcase would be enough to mark the boundary. Moreover, group work during the lunch break should be carried out in the discussion zone only. It would also be advisable to move the computer corner to the far side of the building, if the school can afford to do so. A second round of measurements should be taken after one month.

title: A Complaint About Construction Noise
paragraphs: Dear Mr Pacheco,

I am writing to complain about the level of noise during my recent stay at Hotel Palmar in Cancún, from 3 to 7 July. I booked a double room for four nights at 2,400 pesos per night, a total of 9,600 pesos, after reading the description on your website, which promised a 'peaceful garden retreat'.

Unfortunately, the reality was very different. From seven o'clock every morning, drilling and hammering could be heard from a construction site next door, which belongs, I understand, to the hotel's owners. The noise continued until after five in the afternoon, making it impossible to rest, read or even hold a conversation on the terrace. On the second day, I asked at reception whether I could be moved to a room at the back of the building. I was told that all such rooms were occupied, although the hotel seemed to be half empty. On the third day, the manager's assistant promised to call me back, but he never did.

Had I been informed about the building work when I booked, I would have chosen another hotel. At no point was I offered an apology, a different room or a discount. I was only told that 'this is normal at this time of year', which I do not consider an acceptable answer.
I attach photographs of the site and a short video recorded from my balcony. I would also point out that your website still describes the hotel as peaceful and does not mention the building work.

In view of these circumstances, I request a refund of 4,800 pesos, which corresponds to half the cost of my stay. I believe that this is a fair proposal, given that for part of the time I could at least enjoy the pool and the excellent breakfast, for which I would like to thank your staff. I would also ask you to update the website so that future guests are not misled.
I look forward to receiving your reply within two weeks. I hope that we can resolve this matter without further correspondence.
Yours sincerely,
Ingrid Solano

title: What Is a Zoo For?
focus: Modals of obligation and passive voice
paragraphs: I remember my first visit to the zoo very clearly. I was seven, I had a bag of crisps in my hand, and I stood in front of a tiger that was walking in a straight line along the same ten metres of fence, back and forth, back and forth. Everyone around me laughed and took photographs. I was the only one who felt uncomfortable, and I had no idea why.

Years later, I understood. That pacing, which many animals show in small enclosures, is often interpreted by specialists as a sign of stress. Not every zoo is the same, of course, and some provide spacious areas and good medical care. But I think we should ask a basic question: what is a zoo for?

Defenders of zoos give three answers: education, conservation and entertainment. The first is weaker than it seems. Watch visitors for ten minutes and you will see that many spend only seconds at each enclosure, which is hardly enough to learn anything. The second, conservation, is a genuine achievement in some cases: certain species have been saved from extinction through breeding programmes. The third deserves the least respect, since our amusement should not depend on an animal's discomfort.

So should zoos be closed? Not necessarily. I believe they should change their purpose. Instead of displaying as many species as possible, they could concentrate on a few, keep them in large natural habitats, and focus on rescuing injured wildlife and returning it to the wild. Some places already work this way, and visitors there often say they find the experience more moving, not less.

Naturally, this would cost money. Tickets might become more expensive, and there would be fewer attractions. But we pay without complaint for things we consider valuable. If a ticket cost a few more dollars and meant that no tiger paced along a fence, I, for one, would pay it gladly.
The seven-year-old in front of that tiger knew something that I had forgotten as an adult. Sometimes the most important thing a zoo can teach is that wild animals do not exist to entertain us.
